title: National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2027
official_title: Making appropriations for national security, Department of State, and related programs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Reported by House Appropriations Chair Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart (R-FL-26) on April 30, 2026 as Union Calendar No. 547 (Report No. 119-631) and passed by the House on July 15, 2026. Regular State-Foreign Operations appropriations bills typically require reconciliation with a Senate companion or inclusion in an end-of-year package before enactment; policy riders on UNRWA, the International Criminal Court, the World Health Organization, and Paris Agreement participation are the most likely points of contention in that reconciliation.
summary: This bill provides full-year FY2027 appropriations for the Department of State, USAID successor programs, and related national-security and foreign-assistance accounts. Title I funds the State Department and related programs. Title II funds oversight through the Offices of Inspector General. Title III funds bilateral economic assistance including global health, humanitarian relief, and development programs. Title IV funds international security assistance including foreign military financing and international military training. Title V funds contributions to multilateral development banks and the Global Environment Facility. Title VI funds the Export-Import Bank and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation. Titles VII and VIII carry the bill's policy riders, including preconditions on assistance to the Palestinian Authority, prohibitions on funding UNRWA, the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court, and the Green Climate Fund, and Israel and Egypt assistance floors.
brief: House-passed FY2027 State/Foreign Operations appropriations — $9.76B State Department diplomatic programs, $5.53B PEPFAR, $6.75B Foreign Military Financing (Israel floor $3.30B, Egypt floor $1.30B), and standing prohibitions on funds for UNRWA, the ICJ, the ICC, the Green Climate Fund, and Paris Agreement implementation.

sections.label: Title I — Department of State and Related Programs

items.main: Provides $9.76B for State Department Diplomatic Programs, with $4.16B set aside for Worldwide Security Protection, and $533M in fee-funded Consular and Border Security Program spending.
items.detail: Diplomatic Programs ($9.76B) is allocated across Human Resources ($4.00B, WSP up to $738.55M), Overseas Programs ($1.44B), Diplomatic Policy and Support ($871.6M), and Security Programs ($3.45B, WSP up to $3.42B). Consular and Border Security Programs draws on fees collected under section 7069(e) of the FY2022 SFOPS act (division K of P.L. 117-103) — $533M available until expended, including to reduce passport backlogs and visa wait times. Capital Investment Fund ($413.6M) and Educational and Cultural Exchange Programs ($647M, Fulbright floor $287.8M) are separately appropriated.

items.main: Funds international organizations, commissions, and related U.S. programs including the National Endowment for Democracy ($296.1M) and the East-West Center ($16.7M).
items.detail: National Endowment for Democracy: $296.1M ($197.7M traditional/core institutes, $98.4M democracy programs). Asia Foundation: $17M. East-West Center: $16.7M. International Fisheries Commissions: $75.4M. Congressional-Executive Commission on the PRC: $2.3M. U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission: $4.3M. Israeli Arab Scholarship, Eisenhower Exchange, and the Center for Middle Eastern-Western Dialogue Trust Fund receive only their accrued interest and earnings for FY2027.

sections.label: Title II — Oversight (Offices of Inspector General)

items.main: Appropriates $123.55M for the State Department Office of Inspector General plus $62.5M for the successor OIG with continuing jurisdiction over foreign-assistance programs formerly administered by USAID.
items.detail: State Department OIG: $123.55M (up to $18.5M available through September 30, 2028), notwithstanding section 209(a)(1) of the Foreign Service Act (22 U.S.C. 3929(a)(1)) on post inspections. The successor OIG: $62.5M (up to $9.4M available through September 30, 2028), operating under section 409 of title 5 U.S.C., section 614(f) of the Millennium Challenge Act (22 U.S.C. 7713(f)), section 8A(a) of the Inspector General Act of 1978, section 401 of the Inter-American Foundation Act (22 U.S.C. 290f), and section 505 of the African Development Foundation Act (22 U.S.C. 290h).

items.main: Provides $3.35B for Global Health Programs plus $5.53B for HIV/AIDS activities, including a $1.25B U.S. contribution to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria.
items.detail: Global Health Programs ($3.35B, available through September 30, 2029) covers child survival and maternal health, immunization, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, polio, malaria, neglected tropical diseases, and family planning/reproductive health, apportioned directly to the State Department. HIV/AIDS activities under PEPFAR: $5.53B, including the $1.25B Global Fund contribution and up to $35M for administrative expenses. Standing statutory prohibitions on funding coercive abortion or involuntary sterilization programs and on lobbying for or against abortion are carried forward.

items.main: Provides $5.0B for International Humanitarian Assistance and $100M for the Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund.
items.detail: International Humanitarian Assistance ($5.0B) covers disaster relief under section 491 of the Foreign Assistance Act (of which not less than $2.75B), Migration and Refugee Assistance (22 U.S.C. 2601), and related personnel costs. Not less than $6.5M is set aside for refugees resettling in Israel. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund: $100M, transferrable to International Humanitarian Assistance.

items.main: Provides $6.89B for National Security Investment Programs, $205.2M for the Democracy Fund, $410.5M for the Peace Corps, and $830M for the Millennium Challenge Corporation.
items.detail: National Security Investment Programs ($6.89B) is drawn from sections 103, 105, 106, 214, 251-255, chapter 10 of part I, and chapter 4 of part II of the Foreign Assistance Act, the FREEDOM Support Act, and the SEED Act. Not less than 15% must be made available for programs in Africa. Democracy Fund: $205.2M for the Human Rights and Democracy Fund at the State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor. Peace Corps: $410.5M (of which $7.8M for its OIG). MCC: $830M. A new $100M appropriation is made to the U.S. Foundation for Natural Security and Counterterrorism under section 5102 of the FY2025 NDAA (22 U.S.C. 10602).

items.main: Provides $6.75B for the Foreign Military Financing Program, with statutory floors of $3.30B for Israel, $1.30B for Egypt, and $425M for Jordan.
items.detail: FMF appropriation: $6.75B. Israel: not less than $3.30B in grants, disbursed within 30 days of enactment, of which not less than $250.3M is for in-Israel procurement of defense articles and services. Egypt: not less than $1.30B FMF (within a $1.425B total-assistance floor that also includes $125M in National Security Investment Programs), conditioned on Secretary of State certification that Egypt is sustaining the strategic relationship with the U.S. and meeting its obligations under the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty. Jordan: not less than $1.65B in total assistance, of which not less than $845.1M for budget support and not less than $425M for FMF, plus an additional $400M NSIP for budget support and $50M FMF. Not more than $32M of FMF may be obligated for administering military assistance and sales. Not more than $1.808B of Foreign Military Sales trust-fund receipts may be obligated for administrative expenses under 22 U.S.C. 2792(b) ($30M State Department, $1.778B Defense Department).

items.main: Provides $1.66B for International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement, $870M for Nonproliferation, Anti-terrorism, Demining and Related Programs (NADR), $235M for Security Sector Programs, and $119.2M for International Military Education and Training.
items.detail: INCLE ($1.66B) is drawn from section 481 of the Foreign Assistance Act, with authority to use section 608 excess-property transfers without its normal restrictions. NADR ($870M) covers anti-terrorism assistance, demining, small-arms destruction, a U.S. contribution to the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Preparatory Commission, and a voluntary contribution to the International Atomic Energy Agency (subject to the Israel-participation condition). Security Sector Programs ($235M) is drawn from section 551 of the Foreign Assistance Act and includes not less than $30M for the Multinational Force and Observers in the Sinai. IMET ($119.2M) includes $3.5M for programs to increase the participation of women.

items.main: Provides U.S. contributions to the major multilateral development institutions — $504.0M to the International Development Association, $139.6M to the Global Environment Facility, and $67.5M to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
items.detail: GEF: $139.6M. IDA: $504.0M. Asian Development Fund: $43.6M. African Development Bank paid-in capital: $32.4M, with U.S. Governor authorized to subscribe to callable capital not to exceed $856.2M without fiscal-year limitation. EBRD: $67.5M. Inter-American Investment Corporation: $30M. International Fund for Agricultural Development: $30M. Treasury International Assistance Programs: $50M, of which up to $50M may be used for the cost of loan guarantees to international financial institutions.

sections.label: Title VI — Export and Investment Assistance

items.main: Funds the Export-Import Bank at $125M in administrative expenses (offset to a net $0 general-fund appropriation) and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation at $983.25M gross (net $676.45M), with a $22.0B cap on total DFC loan and guarantee principal outstanding.
items.detail: Export-Import Bank: $8.86M for the OIG, $125M for administrative expenses, $30M for the cost of direct loans, loan guarantees, insurance, and tied-aid grants under section 10 of the Ex-Im Act (available through September 30, 2030); receipts collected under the Ex-Im Act reduce the general-fund appropriation dollar-for-dollar to an estimated $0 net. DFC: $7.2M for the OIG, $983.25M for the Corporate Capital Account ($243M administrative expenses, $740.25M program activities under sections 1421(b),(c),(e),(f),(g) of the BUILD Act), reduced dollar-for-dollar by offsetting collections to a net general-fund appropriation of $676.45M; total loan principal or guaranteed principal is capped at $22.0B. Trade and Development Agency: $87M.

sections.label: Title VII — General Provisions and Policy Riders

items.main: Bars any use of funds for UNRWA, the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court, the World Health Organization (in contravention of Executive Order 14155), the Pandemic Preparedness Accord (until Senate ratification), or the Arms Trade Treaty (until Senate ratification).
items.detail: Sec. 7048(l) prohibits any contribution to the ICJ or the ICC. Sec. 7048(e) prohibits any contribution to UNRWA and any solicitation of UNRWA funds from other donors. Sec. 7049 conditions any U.N. Secretariat funding on written assurance from the Secretary-General that privileges and immunities will not be asserted for UNRWA staff or other U.N. personnel in cases involving gross human-rights violations, terrorism, material support to designated terrorist organizations, or other serious criminal conduct including corruption offenses outside official duties. Sec. 7048(l) also bars funds from supporting iVerify or any similar U.N. fact-checking tool and from any international organization chaired by a Communist Party of China-endorsed PRC national.

items.main: Bars funds for the Green Climate Fund, the Clean Technology Fund, the Loss and Damages Fund, implementation of the Paris Agreement, or support for a carbon tax (Sec. 7061).
items.detail: Sec. 7061(a) codifies the funding restrictions of Executive Order 14162 (Putting America First in International Environmental Agreements). Sec. 7061(b) bars use of funds to impede the uninterrupted transit of hydrocarbons by pipeline under the 1977 U.S.-Canada Transit Pipelines Agreement.

items.main: Sets preconditions on assistance to a new Palestinian state (Sec. 7037), bars any funds for Hamas or the Palestine Liberation Organization (Sec. 7040(f)), and imposes recognition-of-terrorism, oversight, and Taylor Force Act requirements on West Bank and Gaza assistance (Sec. 7039, Sec. 7041(g)).
items.detail: Sec. 7037 bars funds from being provided to support a Palestinian state unless the Secretary of State determines the new governing entity has demonstrated a firm commitment to peaceful co-existence with Israel, is taking measures to counter terrorism and terrorist financing in the West Bank and Gaza, and that the Palestinian Authority is working with other countries in the region toward a just, lasting, and comprehensive Middle East peace. Sec. 7039(c)(1) bars West Bank and Gaza Program funds from being used to recognize or honor individuals who have committed acts of terrorism, or for any educational institution in the West Bank or Gaza named after such an individual. Sec. 7040(f) bars any funds for assistance to Hamas or any entity controlled by Hamas and bars any funds for the Palestine Liberation Organization. Sec. 7041(g)(4) requires that National Security Investment Programs funds made available for the West Bank and Gaza be made available consistent with section 1004(a) of the Taylor Force Act (title X of division S of Public Law 115-141). Sec. 7041(g)(3) imposes Gaza-diversion certifications, third-party monitoring, and quarterly reports on humanitarian assistance for Gaza.

items.main: Bars funds for direct assistance or reparations to Cuba, North Korea, or Iran (Sec. 7007) and bars any government whose duly elected head is deposed by military coup d'etat (Sec. 7008).
items.detail: Sec. 7007 bars any assistance including direct loans, credits, insurance, and Ex-Im guarantees to the governments of Cuba, North Korea, or Iran. Sec. 7008 bars assistance to any country whose duly elected head of government is deposed by military coup d'etat, with resumption permitted after Secretary of State certification of a democratically elected successor government, and with a national-security-interest waiver available on a program-by-program basis. Sec. 7004(e) bars any use of funds to move the U.S. Embassy in Israel to a location other than Jerusalem.

items.main: Iran-specific provisions require sanctions enforcement, semi-annual and 180-day reporting, and bar use of funds to implement the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action or to revoke the IRGC Foreign Terrorist Organization designation (Sec. 7041(b)).
items.detail: Sec. 7041(b)(1) directs use of Diplomatic Programs, NSIP, and NADR funds for preventing Iran from producing a nuclear weapon, responding to U.N. Security Council Resolution violations, and enforcing bilateral and secondary sanctions. Sec. 7041(b)(3) bars any funds from being used to implement an agreement with Iran on its nuclear program or to renew the JCPOA (adopted October 18, 2015) in contravention of the Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act of 2015 (42 U.S.C. 2160e), or to revoke the IRGC's designation as a Foreign Terrorist Organization under 8 U.S.C. 1189.

items.main: Sets the Spending Reduction Account for this Act at $0 (Sec. 8001) and provides the short title `National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2027'.
items.detail: Title VIII contains a single section — the Spending Reduction Account is set at $0, meaning no additional discretionary spending reductions are attributed to this bill beyond those reflected in the titled appropriations.

underreported.section: Section 7061 — Paris Agreement, Green Climate Fund, and Carbon Tax Prohibitions
underreported.summary: The bill bars any funds from being used to implement the Paris Agreement, to contribute to the Green Climate Fund, Clean Technology Fund, or Loss and Damages Fund, or to support the implementation of a carbon tax — codifying the funding restrictions of Executive Order 14162 into appropriations law for FY2027.
underreported.why_unreported: Coverage of annual SFOPS bills tends to focus on the headline Israel and Egypt aid figures. The Sec. 7061 codification converts an executive-order posture on international climate finance into a statutory bar, which persists for the life of the appropriations period regardless of the executive order's status.

underreported.section: Section 7048(l) — International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court Prohibitions
underreported.summary: The bill bars any contribution, grant, or other payment to either the International Court of Justice or the International Criminal Court, notwithstanding any other provision of law.
underreported.why_unreported: Both prohibitions are placed inside a broader `prohibitions on funding' subsection that also covers WHO, the Pandemic Preparedness Accord, iVerify, and the Arms Trade Treaty. The ICJ prohibition in particular is a step beyond prior-year practice, which had focused on the ICC.

underreported.summary: The bill freezes any funding for the U.N. Secretariat or any affiliated U.N. entity until the Secretary of State certifies that the U.N. Secretary-General has provided written assurance that privileges, exemptions, and immunities will not be asserted for UNRWA or other U.N. personnel in cases involving gross human-rights violations, terrorism, material support to terrorist organizations, or other serious criminal conduct.
underreported.why_unreported: The certification requirement effectively conditions all U.N. Secretariat funding on a change in U.N. immunity practice — a broader lever than the direct UNRWA prohibition it accompanies.

underreported.section: Section 7048(l)(7) — Prohibition on International Organizations Chaired by PRC-Endorsed Nationals
underreported.summary: The bill bars any funds from being made available to any international organization chaired by a Communist Party of China-endorsed national of the People's Republic of China.
underreported.why_unreported: This is a novel category of prohibition that applies across the entire international-organizations funding stream in the bill, and its practical scope depends on U.S. determinations about which chairs are `Communist Party of China-endorsed.'

gaps: The Senate has not yet enacted its own FY2027 SFOPS bill, and the Foreign Military Financing floors, UNRWA/ICJ/ICC prohibitions, and Paris Agreement carve-outs in this House-passed text are likely to be renegotiated before enactment.

The bill's $22.0B cap on total U.S. International Development Finance Corporation loan and guarantee principal is a ceiling on lending authority, not an appropriation, and is not counted toward the DFC's $983.25M gross appropriation ($676.45M net) for FY2027.

The Export-Import Bank's $125M administrative expenses and $30M program-budget appropriations are offset dollar-for-dollar by receipts collected under the Ex-Im Act and the Federal Credit Reform Act, resulting in an estimated $0 net general-fund appropriation — the bill does not fix a specific offsetting-collections target.

Sec. 7041(g)(4) applies section 1004(a) of the Taylor Force Act to National Security Investment Programs funds made available for the West Bank and Gaza, but the bill itself does not restate the Taylor Force Act's withholding formula or specify how the required reduction is calculated for the FY2027 appropriation.
